claim: Mu opioid receptor (MOR) agonists directly hyperpolarize a population of neurons in the dorsolateral pons, particularly the Kölliker-Fuse (KF) nucleus.
source: Mu opioid receptor (MOR) agonists directly hyperpolarize a population of neurons in the dorsolateral pons, particularly the Kölliker-Fuse (KF) nucleus, that are key mediators of opioid-induced respiratory depression.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: MOR-expressing KF neurons project to respiratory nuclei in the ventrolateral medulla, including the preBötzinger complex (preBötC) and rostral ventral respiratory group (rVRG).
source: Here, we used retrograde labeling and brain slice electrophysiology to determine that MOR-expressing KF neurons project to respiratory nuclei in the ventrolateral medulla, including the preBötzinger complex (preBötC) and rostral ventral respiratory group (rVRG).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from retrograde labeling experiments shown in Figures 2, 4, and 5.

claim: Medullary-projecting, MOR-expressing dorsolateral pontine neurons express FoxP2.
source: These medullary-projecting, MOR-expressing dorsolateral pontine neurons express FoxP2 and are distinct from calcitonin gene-related peptide-expressing lateral parabrachial neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Medullary-projecting, MOR-expressing dorsolateral pontine neurons are distinct from calcitonin gene-related peptide-expressing lateral parabrachial neurons.
source: These medullary-projecting, MOR-expressing dorsolateral pontine neurons express FoxP2 and are distinct from calcitonin gene-related peptide-expressing lateral parabrachial neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Dorsolateral pontine neurons release glutamate onto excitatory preBötC and rVRG neurons via monosynaptic projections.
source: Furthermore, dorsolateral pontine neurons release glutamate onto excitatory preBötC and rVRG neurons via monosynaptic projections, which is inhibited by presynaptic opioid receptors.
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic stimulation and electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Glutamate release from dorsolateral pontine neurons onto excitatory preBötC and rVRG neurons is inhibited by presynaptic opioid receptors.
source: Furthermore, dorsolateral pontine neurons release glutamate onto excitatory preBötC and rVRG neurons via monosynaptic projections, which is inhibited by presynaptic opioid receptors.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data showing ME-induced reduction in oEPSC amplitude and increased paired-pulse ratio in Figure 3.

claim: The majority of excitatory preBötC and rVRG neurons receiving MOR-sensitive glutamatergic synaptic input from the dorsolateral pons are themselves hyperpolarized by opioids.
source: Surprisingly, the majority of excitatory preBötC and rVRG neurons receiving MOR-sensitive glutamatergic synaptic input from the dorsolateral pons are themselves hyperpolarized by opioids, suggesting a selective opioid-sensitive circuit from the KF to the ventrolateral medulla.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data showing ME-induced outward currents in 68% of preBötC neurons and 88% of rVRG neurons in Figure 3G, H, L, and M.

claim: Opioids inhibit the excitatory pontomedullary respiratory circuit by three distinct mechanisms: somatodendritic MORs on dorsolateral pontine neurons, presynaptic MORs on dorsolateral pontine neuron terminals in the ventrolateral medulla, and somatodendritic MORs on ventrolateral medullary neurons.
source: Opioids inhibit this excitatory pontomedullary respiratory circuit by three distinct mechanisms—somatodendritic MORs on dorsolateral pontine and ventrolateral medullary neurons and presynaptic MORs on dorsolateral pontine neuron terminals in the ventrolateral medulla—all of which could contribute to opioid-induced respiratory depression.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from Figures 3 and 4 showing opioid effects at multiple sites.

claim: The Kölliker-Fuse (KF) nucleus and adjacent lateral parabrachial area (LPB) of the dorsolateral pons are critical to the neural control of breathing.
source: The Kölliker-Fuse (KF) nucleus and adjacent lateral parabrachial area (LPB) of the dorsolateral pons are critical to the neural control of breathing (Lumsden, 1923; Fung and St John, 1995; Dutschmann and Herbert, 2006; Smith et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The KF/LPB is composed of a heterogeneous population of respiratory neurons that impact respiratory rate and pattern.
source: The KF/LPB is composed of a heterogeneous population of respiratory neurons that impact respiratory rate and pattern (Chamberlin and Saper, 1994; Navarrete-Opazo et al., 2020; Saunders and Levitt, 2020) via excitatory projections to respiratory nuclei in the ventrolateral medulla, including, but not limited to the Bötzinger complex (BötC), preBötzinger complex (preBötC), and rostral ventral respiratory group (rVRG) (Song et al., 2012; Yokota et al., 2015; Geerling et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The KF/LPB impacts respiratory rate and pattern via excitatory projections to respiratory nuclei in the ventrolateral medulla, including the BötC, preBötC, and rVRG.
source: The KF/LPB is composed of a heterogeneous population of respiratory neurons that impact respiratory rate and pattern (Chamberlin and Saper, 1994; Navarrete-Opazo et al., 2020; Saunders and Levitt, 2020) via excitatory projections to respiratory nuclei in the ventrolateral medulla, including, but not limited to the Bötzinger complex (BötC), preBötzinger complex (preBötC), and rostral ventral respiratory group (rVRG) (Song et al., 2012; Yokota et al., 2015; Geerling et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The preBötC generates inspiratory rhythm.
source: The preBötC generates inspiratory rhythm (Smith et al., 1991), which is relayed to inspiratory premotor neurons in the rVRG.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Smith et al., 1991).

claim: Inspiratory rhythm generated by the preBötC is relayed to inspiratory premotor neurons in the rVRG.
source: The preBötC generates inspiratory rhythm (Smith et al., 1991), which is relayed to inspiratory premotor neurons in the rVRG.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of respiratory circuitry.

claim: The BötC contains mostly inhibitory neurons that fire during expiration and is a major source of inhibition within the respiratory network.
source: The BötC contains mostly inhibitory neurons that fire during expiration and is a major source of inhibition within the network (Schreihofer et al., 1999; Ezure et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The dynamic interplay between the KF/LPB and the BötC, preBötC, and rVRG is essential for optimized respiratory output.
source: The dynamic interplay between the KF/LPB and the BötC, preBötC, and rVRG is essential for optimized respiratory output (Dutschmann and Dick, 2012; Smith et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: All respiratory nuclei (KF/LPB, BötC, preBötC, and rVRG) express MORs.
source: Unfortunately, all of these respiratory nuclei express MORs, leading to inhibition of the control of breathing network via multiple potential sites and mechanisms (Gray et al., 1999; Lonergan et al., 2003; Montandon et al., 2011; Levitt et al., 2015; Cinelli et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The dorsolateral pontine KF/LPB and the preBötC of the ventrolateral medulla are considered critical for opioid-induced respiratory depression.
source: Two respiratory nuclei considered critical for opioid-induced respiratory depression are the KF/LPB of the dorsolateral pons and the preBötC of the ventrolateral medulla (Bachmutsky et al., 2020; Varga et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Deletion of MORs from the KF/LPB attenuates morphine-induced respiratory depression.
source: The dorsolateral pontine KF/LPB is considered a key contributor of opioid-induced respiratory depression because (1) deletion of MORs from the KF/LPB attenuates morphine-induced respiratory depression (Bachmutsky et al., 2020; Varga et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021), (2) opioids injected into the KF/LPB reduce respiratory rate (Prkic et al., 2012; Levitt et al., 2015; Miller et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2021), (3) blockade of KF/LPB opioid receptors rescues fentanyl-induced apnea (Saunders and Levitt, 2020), and (4) chemogenetic inhibition of MOR-expressing LPB neurons induces respiratory depression (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Opioids injected into the KF/LPB reduce respiratory rate.
source: The dorsolateral pontine KF/LPB is considered a key contributor of opioid-induced respiratory depression because (1) deletion of MORs from the KF/LPB attenuates morphine-induced respiratory depression (Bachmutsky et al., 2020; Varga et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021), (2) opioids injected into the KF/LPB reduce respiratory rate (Prkic et al., 2012; Levitt et al., 2015; Miller et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2021), (3) blockade of KF/LPB opioid receptors rescues fentanyl-induced apnea (Saunders and Levitt, 2020), and (4) chemogenetic inhibition of MOR-expressing LPB neurons induces respiratory depression (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Blockade of KF/LPB opioid receptors rescues fentanyl-induced apnea.
source: The dorsolateral pontine KF/LPB is considered a key contributor of opioid-induced respiratory depression because (1) deletion of MORs from the KF/LPB attenuates morphine-induced respiratory depression (Bachmutsky et al., 2020; Varga et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021), (2) opioids injected into the KF/LPB reduce respiratory rate (Prkic et al., 2012; Levitt et al., 2015; Miller et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2021), (3) blockade of KF/LPB opioid receptors rescues fentanyl-induced apnea (Saunders and Levitt, 2020), and (4) chemogenetic inhibition of MOR-expressing LPB neurons induces respiratory depression (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of MOR-expressing LPB neurons induces respiratory depression.
source: The dorsolateral pontine KF/LPB is considered a key contributor of opioid-induced respiratory depression because (1) deletion of MORs from the KF/LPB attenuates morphine-induced respiratory depression (Bachmutsky et al., 2020; Varga et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021), (2) opioids injected into the KF/LPB reduce respiratory rate (Prkic et al., 2012; Levitt et al., 2015; Miller et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2021), (3) blockade of KF/LPB opioid receptors rescues fentanyl-induced apnea (Saunders and Levitt, 2020), and (4) chemogenetic inhibition of MOR-expressing LPB neurons induces respiratory depression (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: MORs inhibit neurotransmission by hyperpolarizing neurons through activation of somatodendritic GIRK channels.
source: MORs inhibit neurotransmission by hyperpolarizing neurons through activation of somatodendritic GIRK channels and/or inhibiting presynaptic neurotransmitter release through inhibition of voltage-gated calcium channels (Jiang and North, 1992; Chahl, 1996; Zamponi and Snutch, 1998; Al-Hasani and Bruchas, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: MORs inhibit presynaptic neurotransmitter release through inhibition of voltage-gated calcium channels.
source: MORs inhibit neurotransmission by hyperpolarizing neurons through activation of somatodendritic GIRK channels and/or inhibiting presynaptic neurotransmitter release through inhibition of voltage-gated calcium channels (Jiang and North, 1992; Chahl, 1996; Zamponi and Snutch, 1998; Al-Hasani and Bruchas, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Presynaptic MORs inhibit synaptic transmission in the preBötC.
source: In the preBötC, presynaptic MORs inhibit synaptic transmission (Ballanyi et al., 2010; Wei and Ramirez, 2019; Baertsch et al., 2021) and are expressed more abundantly than somatodendritic MORs (Lonergan et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Presynaptic MORs are expressed more abundantly than somatodendritic MORs in the preBötC.
source: In the preBötC, presynaptic MORs inhibit synaptic transmission (Ballanyi et al., 2010; Wei and Ramirez, 2019; Baertsch et al., 2021) and are expressed more abundantly than somatodendritic MORs (Lonergan et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Opioids hyperpolarize a subset of KF neurons.
source: Opioids hyperpolarize a subset of KF neurons (Levitt et al., 2015), whose neurochemical identity and possible projection targets are unknown.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Glutamatergic KF neurons project to the ventrolateral medulla.
source: Glutamatergic KF neurons project to the ventrolateral medulla (Song et al., 2012; Yokota et al., 2015; Geerling et al., 2017) and, if inhibited by opioids—either by somatodendritic activation of GIRK channels and/or presynaptic inhibition of neurotransmitter release—could depress breathing.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: MOR-expressing neurons and neurites were identified in the dorsolateral pons, specifically in the lateral parabrachial area and KF in Oprm1-tdT mice.
source: MOR-expressing neurons and neurites were identified in the dorsolateral pons, specifically in the lateral parabrachial area and KF (n = 3; Figure 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A-D.

claim: MOR-expressing neurons were identified in the lateral parabrachial and KF areas following injection of AAV-DIO-GFP into the dorsolateral pons of adult Oprm1Cre/+ mice.
source: MOR-expressing neurons were again identified in the lateral parabrachial and KF areas (Figure 1E–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E-H.

claim: MORs are expressed in LPB.
source: These results are consistent with previous studies showing that MORs are expressed in LPB (Huang et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021) and KF (Levitt et al., 2015; Varga et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: MORs are expressed in KF.
source: These results are consistent with previous studies showing that MORs are expressed in LPB (Huang et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021) and KF (Levitt et al., 2015; Varga et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Oprm1+ dorsolateral pontine neurons and neurites were retrogradely labeled from both preBötC and rVRG.
source: Oprm1+ dorsolateral pontine neurons and neurites were retrogradely labeled from both preBötC and rVRG (Figure 2D–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D-I.

claim: Oprm1+ projections to the preBötC and the rVRG were mostly localized to the rostral and mid-rostral KF, and nearly absent in the caudal KF and lateral parabrachial area.
source: Interestingly, Oprm1+ projections to the preBötC (Figure 2D–F; n = 5) and the rVRG (Figure 2G–I; n = 5) were mostly localized to the rostral and mid-rostral KF, and nearly absent in the caudal KF and lateral parabrachial area (Figure 2F and I).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D-I.

claim: The majority of the retrogradely labeled dorsolateral pontine neurons and neurites were ipsilateral to the injection site, with very few or no contralateral neurons or neurites expressing GFP.
source: The majority of the retrogradely labeled dorsolateral pontine neurons and neurites were ipsilateral to the injection site, with very few or no contralateral neurons or neurites expressing GFP.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the retrograde labeling experiments.

claim: Qualitatively fewer Oprm1+ KF neurons projected to the BötC compared to preBötC and rVRG projections.
source: In contrast to preBötC and rVRG projections, qualitatively fewer Oprm1+ KF neurons projected to the BötC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E-G.

claim: KF neurons projecting to the ventrolateral medulla are glutamatergic.
source: Given that KF neurons projecting to the ventrolateral medulla are glutamatergic (Geerling et al., 2017) and express MORs (Figure 2), we hypothesized that opioids inhibit glutamate release from KF terminals onto respiratory neurons in the ventrolateral medulla, particularly the preBötC and rVRG.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of KF terminals drove pharmacologically isolated excitatory postsynaptic currents (oEPSCs) in excitatory preBötC and rVRG neurons.
source: Optogenetic stimulation of KF terminals drove pharmacologically isolated excitatory postsynaptic currents (oEPSCs) in excitatory preBötC and rVRG neurons (Figure 3D and I) that were blocked by the AMPA-type glutamate receptor antagonist 6,7-dinitroquinoxaline-2,3-dione (DNQX; 10 μM; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B, n = 11).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3D, I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: oEPSCs driven by optogenetic stimulation of KF terminals were blocked by DNQX.
source: Optogenetic stimulation of KF terminals drove pharmacologically isolated excitatory postsynaptic currents (oEPSCs) in excitatory preBötC and rVRG neurons (Figure 3D and I) that were blocked by the AMPA-type glutamate receptor antagonist 6,7-dinitroquinoxaline-2,3-dione (DNQX; 10 μM; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B, n = 11).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: KF synapses onto medullary respiratory neurons are monosynaptic.
source: Additionally, KF synapses onto medullary respiratory neurons are monosynaptic because oEPSCs were eliminated by tetrodotoxin (TTX; 1 μM) yet restored by subsequent application of 4-aminopyridine (4AP; 100 μM) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and C; n = 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, C.

claim: ME (3 μM) decreased the oEPSC amplitude in preBötC neurons.
source: ME (3 μM) decreased the oEPSC amplitude in preBötC neurons (Figure 3D and E; n = 13) and in rVRG neurons (Figure 3I and J; n = 9), which reversed when ME was washed from the slice.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3D, E.

claim: ME (3 μM) decreased the oEPSC amplitude in rVRG neurons.
source: ME (3 μM) decreased the oEPSC amplitude in preBötC neurons (Figure 3D and E; n = 13) and in rVRG neurons (Figure 3I and J; n = 9), which reversed when ME was washed from the slice.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3I, J.

claim: ME increased the paired-pulse ratio (PPR) in preBötC neurons.
source: In addition, ME increased the paired-pulse ratio (PPR) in both preBötC (Figure 3F; n = 11) and rVRG neurons (Figure 3K; n = 9), indicating inhibition of glutamate release by presynaptic MORs.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: ME increased the paired-pulse ratio (PPR) in rVRG neurons.
source: In addition, ME increased the paired-pulse ratio (PPR) in both preBötC (Figure 3F; n = 11) and rVRG neurons (Figure 3K; n = 9), indicating inhibition of glutamate release by presynaptic MORs.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Increased paired-pulse ratio indicates inhibition of glutamate release by presynaptic MORs.
source: In addition, ME increased the paired-pulse ratio (PPR) in both preBötC (Figure 3F; n = 11) and rVRG neurons (Figure 3K; n = 9), indicating inhibition of glutamate release by presynaptic MORs.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge that increased PPR indicates presynaptic inhibition.

claim: oEPSCs were inhibited by ME by at least 30% in nearly all preBötC neurons (11 of 13 neurons).
source: The proportion of opioid-sensitive KF terminals was surprisingly high, considering that oEPSCs were inhibited by ME by a threshold of at least 30% in nearly all preBötC neurons (11 of 13 neurons) and all rVRG neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from Figure 3.

claim: oEPSCs were inhibited by ME by at least 30% in all rVRG neurons tested.
source: The proportion of opioid-sensitive KF terminals was surprisingly high, considering that oEPSCs were inhibited by ME by a threshold of at least 30% in nearly all preBötC neurons (11 of 13 neurons) and all rVRG neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from Figure 3.

claim: Presynaptic opioid receptors inhibit glutamate release from KF terminals onto 91% (20 of 22 neurons) of excitatory preBötC and rVRG neurons.
source: Thus, presynaptic opioid receptors inhibit glutamate release from KF terminals onto a majority of excitatory preBötC and rVRG neurons (91% [20 of 22 neurons]).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from Figure 3.

claim: ME (3 μM) induced an outward current in 68% of preBötC neurons (8 of 12 neurons).
source: ME (3 μM) induced an outward current in 68% of preBötC neurons (8 of 12 neurons) (Figure 3G and H) and 88% of rVRG neurons (7 of 8 neurons) (Figure 3L and M).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3G, H.

claim: ME (3 μM) induced an outward current in 88% of rVRG neurons (7 of 8 neurons).
source: ME (3 μM) induced an outward current in 68% of preBötC neurons (8 of 12 neurons) (Figure 3G and H) and 88% of rVRG neurons (7 of 8 neurons) (Figure 3L and M).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3L, M.

claim: There was no difference in the amplitude of the ME-mediated current in preBötC and rVRG neurons.
source: There was no difference in the amplitude of the ME-mediated current in preBötC and rVRG neurons (p=0.294; unpaired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiology data.

claim: A majority of excitatory preBötC and rVRG neurons that receive opioid-sensitive glutamatergic synapses from KF neurons are themselves hyperpolarized by opioids.
source: Thus, a majority of excitatory preBötC and rVRG neurons that receive opioid-sensitive glutamatergic synapses from KF neurons are themselves hyperpolarized by opioids, indicating both pre- and postsynaptic suppression of this excitatory synapse by opioids.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from Figure 3.

claim: Opioids hyperpolarize approximately 60% of KF neurons by activating GIRK channels.
source: Opioids hyperpolarize a subpopulation (~60%) of KF neurons by activating G protein-coupled inwardly rectifying potassium (GIRK) channels (Levitt et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: ME induced an outward current in 59% (13 of 22 neurons) of KF neurons that project to the preBötC.
source: ME induced an outward current in 59% (13 of 22 neurons) of KF neurons that project to the preBötC (Figure 4E) and 67% (12 of 18 neurons) of KF neurons that project to the rVRG (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: ME induced an outward current in 67% (12 of 18 neurons) of KF neurons that project to the rVRG.
source: ME induced an outward current in 59% (13 of 22 neurons) of KF neurons that project to the preBötC (Figure 4E) and 67% (12 of 18 neurons) of KF neurons that project to the rVRG (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The average amplitude of the ME-mediated current was not different between KF neurons that project to preBötC or rVRG.
source: The average amplitude of the ME-mediated current was not different between KF neurons that project to preBötC (n = 13) or rVRG (n = 12) (p=0.8250; unpaired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiology data.

claim: Both opioid-sensitive and non-sensitive KF neurons project to preBötC and rVRG.
source: Thus, both opioid-sensitive and non-sensitive KF neurons project to preBötC and rVRG, with a proportion similar to the general population of KF neurons with unidentified projection targets (Levitt et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from Figure 4 and comparison to prior research.

claim: ME induced an outward current in only 36% (4 of 11 neurons) of KF neurons that project to the BötC.
source: We made whole-cell voltage-clamp recordings from fluorescent KF neurons and found that ME induced an outward current in only 36% (4 of 11 neurons) of KF neurons that project to the BötC (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A lower proportion of opioid-sensitive neurons project to BötC compared to preBötC and rVRG.
source: Thus, a lower proportion of opioid-sensitive neurons project to BötC compared to preBötC and rVRG.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of electrophysiology data from Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There were significantly more retrograde-labeled neurons in rostral and mid-rostral slices, regardless of Oprm1 expression status.
source: There were significantly more retrograde-labeled neurons in rostral and mid-rostral slices, regardless of Oprm1 expression status (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Retrograde-labeled Oprm1+ neurons were mostly localized to the rostral and mid-rostral slices, and not in caudal slices or lateral parabrachial area.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Figure 2), retrograde-labeled Oprm1+ neurons were mostly localized to the rostral and mid-rostral slices, and not in caudal slices or lateral parabrachial area (Figure 5C and E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C, E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The percentage of retrograde-labeled neurons that were Oprm1+ in rostral slices (56%) and mid-rostral slices (47%) was higher than in caudal slices (15%).
source: The percentage of retrograde-labeled neurons that were Oprm1+ (co-labeled with mCherry and GFP) in rostral slices (56%) and mid-rostral slices (47%) was higher than in caudal slices (15%) (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Oprm1+ and Oprm1- KF neurons that project to respiratory nuclei in the ventrolateral medulla are distributed to the rostral and mid-rostral regions of the KF of mice.
source: Taken together, Oprm1+ and Oprm1- KF neurons that project to respiratory nuclei in the ventrolateral medulla are distributed to the rostral and mid-rostral regions of the KF of mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from Figure 5.

claim: Rostral glutamatergic KF neurons express FoxP2.
source: Rostral glutamatergic KF neurons express FoxP2 (Forkhead box protein P2) (Geerling et al., 2017; Karthik et al., 2022), whereas MOR-expressing glutamatergic neurons in the external lateral parabrachial subnucleus that project to the forebrain express Calca, a gene that encodes the neuropeptide calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) (Huang et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: MOR-expressing glutamatergic neurons in the external lateral parabrachial subnucleus that project to the forebrain express Calca, a gene that encodes CGRP.
source: Rostral glutamatergic KF neurons express FoxP2 (Forkhead box protein P2) (Geerling et al., 2017; Karthik et al., 2022), whereas MOR-expressing glutamatergic neurons in the external lateral parabrachial subnucleus that project to the forebrain express Calca, a gene that encodes the neuropeptide calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) (Huang et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Oprm1+, medullary-projecting KF neurons expressed FoxP2.
source: Oprm1+, medullary-projecting KF neurons expressed FoxP2 (n = 3; Figure 6), consistent with the population of glutamatergic FoxP2 and Lmx1b neurons in the rostral KF (Karthik et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Oprm1+, medullary-projecting KF neurons are consistent with the population of glutamatergic FoxP2 and Lmx1b neurons in the rostral KF.
source: Oprm1+, medullary-projecting KF neurons expressed FoxP2 (n = 3; Figure 6), consistent with the population of glutamatergic FoxP2 and Lmx1b neurons in the rostral KF (Karthik et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to prior research.

claim: FoxP2-expressing Oprm1+, medullary-projecting neurons are a separate population from FoxP2-expressing neurons located more dorsally and caudally in the inner portion of the external lateral parabrachial area and those activated by sodium deprivation.
source: These are a separate population from FoxP2-expressing neurons located more dorsally and caudally in the inner portion of the external lateral parabrachial area and those activated by sodium deprivation (Geerling et al., 2011; Karthik et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison to prior research and anatomical location.

claim: FoxP2 expression overlapped with a smaller population of Oprm1+ medullary-projecting neurons in the caudal KF, which contains GABAergic neurons.
source: FoxP2 expression also overlapped with a smaller population of Oprm1+ medullary-projecting neurons in the caudal KF, which contains GABAergic neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Geerling et al., 2017; Karthik et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and citations to prior research.

claim: FoxP2 was not detected in the outer portion of the external lateral parabrachial subnucleus.
source: FoxP2 was not detected in the outer portion of the external lateral parabrachial subnucleus (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), consistent with previous findings (Geerling et al., 2011; Karthik et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and citations to prior research.

claim: Oprm1+, medullary-projecting KF neurons did not express CGRP.
source: Oprm1+, medullary-projecting KF neurons did not express CGRP (n = 3; Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7.

claim: CGRP expression was robust in external lateral parabrachial neurons and their axon fiber projections.
source: Although CGRP expression was absent from the rostral KF and medullary-projecting Oprm1+ neurons and neurites, it was robust in external lateral parabrachial neurons and their axon fiber projections (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7C, D.

claim: KF neurons were more likely inhibited by presynaptic vs. somatodendritic MORs.
source: Unexpectedly, KF neurons were more likely inhibited by presynaptic vs. somatodendritic MORs.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of data from Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The vast majority of KF terminals expressed presynaptic MORs since opioids inhibited glutamate release onto 91% of preBötC and rVRG neurons.
source: The vast majority of KF terminals expressed presynaptic MORs since opioids inhibited glutamate release onto 91% of preBötC and rVRG neurons (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is based on data from Figure 3.

claim: Postsynaptic (somatodendritic) MOR-mediated outward currents were only observed in about two-thirds of medullary-projecting KF neurons.
source: In contrast, postsynaptic (somatodendritic) MOR-mediated outward currents were only observed in about two-thirds of medullary-projecting KF neurons (Figure 4), which matches prior studies without projection identification (Levitt et al., 2015; Varga et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is based on data from Figure 4 and comparison to prior research.

claim: The percentage of retrograde-labeled neurons that were Oprm1+ (56% in rostral and 47% in mid-rostral slices) nearly matched the percentages of functionally identified opioid-sensitive KF neurons (59% of preBötC-projecting and 67% of rVRG-projecting neurons).
source: However, this seems unlikely since the percentage of retrograde-labeled neurons that were Oprm1+ (56% in rostral and 47% in mid-rostral slices; Figure 5) nearly matched the percentages of functionally identified opioid-sensitive KF neurons (59% of preBötC-projecting and 67% of rVRG-projecting neurons; Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of data from Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Opioid-sensitive glutamatergic KF neurons preferentially synapse onto excitatory medullary neurons, while non-opioidergic KF neurons might preferentially synapse onto non-excitatory (i.e. inhibitory) medullary neurons.
source: The last and most interesting possibility is that opioid-sensitive glutamatergic KF neurons preferentially synapse onto excitatory medullary neurons, while non-opioidergic KF neurons might preferentially synapse onto non-excitatory (i.e. inhibitory) medullary neurons.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from the data.

claim: KF neurons project to excitatory and, to a lesser extent, inhibitory preBötC neurons.
source: This hypothesis is consistent with anatomical-tracing studies showing that KF neurons project to excitatory and, to a lesser extent, inhibitory preBötC neurons (Yang et al., 2020), and could be tested by recording from labeled inhibitory neurons in the ventrolateral medulla.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Inspiratory dorsolateral pontine neurons are silenced by fentanyl, whereas expiratory neurons are not.
source: We have recently found that inspiratory dorsolateral pontine neurons are silenced by fentanyl, whereas expiratory neurons are not (Saunders et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to recent research.

claim: A higher proportion of opioid-insensitive pontine neurons projected to the BötC.
source: This could include opioid-insensitive KF neurons that project to inhibitory neurons in the BötC since a higher proportion of opioid-insensitive pontine neurons projected to the BötC (Figure 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on data from Figure 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The NTS contains abundant MOR-expressing afferents and non-MOR-expressing neurons that are activated by disinhibition during opioid exposure.
source: Inhibitory input could also come from the NTS, which contains abundant MOR-expressing afferents and non-MOR-expressing neurons that are activated by disinhibition during opioid exposure (Glatzer et al., 2007; Maletz et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The external lateral parabrachial subnucleus expresses Lmx1b and CGRP, but not FoxP2.
source: The most well-defined area in the dorsolateral pons is the external lateral parabrachial subnucleus, which expresses Lmx1b and CGRP, but not FoxP2 (Karthik et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CGRP-expressing external lateral parabrachial neurons project primarily to the forebrain.
source: CGRP-expressing external lateral parabrachial neurons project primarily to the forebrain (Huang et al., 2021) and are involved in pain processing, feeding, and CO2-induced arousal (Campos et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2018; Kaur et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CGRP-expressing external lateral parabrachial neurons are involved in pain processing, feeding, and CO2-induced arousal.
source: CGRP-expressing external lateral parabrachial neurons project primarily to the forebrain (Huang et al., 2021) and are involved in pain processing, feeding, and CO2-induced arousal (Campos et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2018; Kaur et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: MORs are highly co-expressed with CGRP in external lateral parabrachial neurons.
source: Although MORs are highly co-expressed with CGRP in these neurons (Huang et al., 2021), we did not observe opioid-sensitive or Oprm1+retrograde-labeled neurons in the external lateral parabrachial area.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Electrophysiologically or histologically identified opioid-sensitive/Oprm1+ neurons that project to the ventrolateral medulla were found rostrally and ventrally in the area overlapping FoxP2 expression in the KF.
source: Rather, electrophysiologically or histologically identified opioid-sensitive/Oprm1+ neurons that project to the ventrolateral medulla were found rostrally and ventrally in the area overlapping FoxP2 expression in the KF.
evidence: The claim is based on data from Figures 4, 5, and 6.

claim: At least two distinct subpopulations of Oprm1+ dorsolateral pontine neurons exist that can be distinguished based on CGRP expression and projection pattern: forebrain-projecting CGRP-expressing neurons and medullary-projecting neurons that do not express CGRP.
source: Thus, at least two distinct subpopulations of Oprm1+ dorsolateral pontine neurons exist that can be distinguished based on CGRP expression and projection pattern: forebrain-projecting CGRP-expressing neurons and medullary-projecting neurons that do not express CGRP.
evidence: The claim is based on data from Figure 7 and comparison to prior research.

claim: Both forebrain-projecting CGRP-expressing and medullary-projecting non-CGRP-expressing Oprm1+ pontine neurons are involved in pain and breathing due to reciprocal excitatory synaptic connections.
source: Both populations are involved in pain and breathing due, at least in part, to reciprocal excitatory synaptic connections (Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Medullary-projecting Oprm1+ pontine neurons can be involved in pain processing, but not to the same extent as forebrain-projecting Oprm1/CGRP+ pontine neurons.
source: Although medullary-projecting Oprm1+ pontine neurons did not express CGRP (Figure 7), they can still be involved in pain processing, just not to the same extent as forebrain-projecting Oprm1/CGRP+ pontine neurons (Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is based on data from Figure 7 and comparison to prior research.

claim: Both forebrain-projecting and medullary-projecting populations of Oprm1+ dorsolateral pontine neurons are likely involved in opioid-induced respiratory depression.
source: Both populations of Oprm1+ dorsolateral pontine neurons are also likely involved in opioid-induced respiratory depression.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from the data and prior research.

claim: MORs in glutamatergic medullary-projecting rostral KF neurons could reduce respiratory rate by decreasing excitatory input to the preBötC and rVRG.
source: MORs in glutamatergic medullary-projecting rostral KF neurons could reduce respiratory rate by decreasing excitatory input to the preBötC and rVRG (Figure 3), leading to a distributed blunting effect on inspiration-generating processes within the ventrolateral medulla.
evidence: The claim is based on data from Figure 3 and inference about mechanism.

claim: MORs in forebrain-projecting pontine neurons could reduce respiratory rate through intra-pontine excitatory connections with medullary-projecting MOR+ pontine neurons.
source: In contrast, MORs in forebrain-projecting pontine neurons could reduce respiratory rate through intra-pontine excitatory connections with medullary-projecting MOR+ pontine neurons (Liu et al., 2022) or through reduced excitatory input to forebrain areas involved in arousal (Kaur et al., 2017), which may be especially important in sleep-dependent effects of opioids on breathing (Montandon and Horner, 2019).
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on citations to prior research.

claim: MORs in forebrain-projecting pontine neurons could reduce respiratory rate through reduced excitatory input to forebrain areas involved in arousal.
source: In contrast, MORs in forebrain-projecting pontine neurons could reduce respiratory rate through intra-pontine excitatory connections with medullary-projecting MOR+ pontine neurons (Liu et al., 2022) or through reduced excitatory input to forebrain areas involved in arousal (Kaur et al., 2017), which may be especially important in sleep-dependent effects of opioids on breathing (Montandon and Horner, 2019).
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on citations to prior research.

claim: Presynaptic opioid receptors in the preBötC inhibit synaptic transmission.
source: Presynaptic opioid receptors in the preBötC inhibit synaptic transmission and have been postulated to disrupt preBötC neuron bursting (Ballanyi et al., 2010; Wei and Ramirez, 2019; Baertsch et al., 2021) by inhibition of excitatory neurotransmission that is dominant during bursts (Ashhad and Feldman, 2020), but the projection-specific location(s) of these presynaptic MORs is unknown.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Presynaptic opioid receptors in the preBötC have been postulated to disrupt preBötC neuron bursting by inhibition of excitatory neurotransmission that is dominant during bursts.
source: Presynaptic opioid receptors in the preBötC inhibit synaptic transmission and have been postulated to disrupt preBötC neuron bursting (Ballanyi et al., 2010; Wei and Ramirez, 2019; Baertsch et al., 2021) by inhibition of excitatory neurotransmission that is dominant during bursts (Ashhad and Feldman, 2020), but the projection-specific location(s) of these presynaptic MORs is unknown.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Only a subpopulation of preBötC neurons contain MORs.
source: Only a subpopulation of preBötC neurons contain MORs (Bachmutsky et al., 2020; Baertsch et al., 2021; Kallurkar et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The population of MOR-expressing preBötC neurons is heterogeneous, including nearly equal numbers of glutamatergic, GABAergic, and glycinergic neurons.
source: The population of MOR-expressing preBötC neurons is heterogeneous, including nearly equal numbers of glutamatergic, GABAergic, and glycinergic neurons (Bachmutsky et al., 2020), type 1 and type 2 Dbx1-expressing inspiratory neurons (Kallurkar et al., 2022), and pre-inspiratory, inspiratory, expiratory, and tonic neurons (Baertsch et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: MOR-expressing preBötC neurons include type 1 and type 2 Dbx1-expressing inspiratory neurons.
source: The population of MOR-expressing preBötC neurons is heterogeneous, including nearly equal numbers of glutamatergic, GABAergic, and glycinergic neurons (Bachmutsky et al., 2020), type 1 and type 2 Dbx1-expressing inspiratory neurons (Kallurkar et al., 2022), and pre-inspiratory, inspiratory, expiratory, and tonic neurons (Baertsch et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: MOR-expressing preBötC neurons include pre-inspiratory, inspiratory, expiratory, and tonic neurons.
source: The population of MOR-expressing preBötC neurons is heterogeneous, including nearly equal numbers of glutamatergic, GABAergic, and glycinergic neurons (Bachmutsky et al., 2020), type 1 and type 2 Dbx1-expressing inspiratory neurons (Kallurkar et al., 2022), and pre-inspiratory, inspiratory, expiratory, and tonic neurons (Baertsch et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: MOR-expressing dorsolateral pontine glutamatergic inputs seem to preferentially synapse onto MOR-expressing excitatory preBötC neurons.
source: We found that MOR-expressing dorsolateral pontine glutamatergic inputs seem to preferentially synapse onto MOR-expressing excitatory preBötC neurons since 68% of preBötC neurons (8 of 12 neurons) that received glutamatergic input from the dorsolateral pons were hyperpolarized by opioid (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is based on data from Figure 3G and inference.

claim: MOR-expressing glutamatergic preBötC neurons are important mediators of inspiratory rhythm generation and opioid-induced respiratory depression in medullary slices.
source: This percentage is higher than even the highest estimate of MOR-expressing preBötC neurons (Baertsch et al., 2021), suggesting dorsolateral pontine neurons preferentially target MOR-expressing glutamatergic preBötC neurons, which are important mediators of inspiratory rhythm generation and opioid-induced respiratory depression in medullary slices (Sun et al., 2019; Bachmutsky et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Postsynaptic, but not presynaptic, opioid receptors couple to GIRK channels.
source: For instance, postsynaptic, but not presynaptic, opioid receptors couple to GIRK channels (Lüscher et al., 1997) through binding of up to four Gβγ subunits directly to the channel (Whorton and MacKinnon, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Postsynaptic opioid receptors couple to GIRK channels through binding of up to four Gβγ subunits directly to the channel.
source: For instance, postsynaptic, but not presynaptic, opioid receptors couple to GIRK channels (Lüscher et al., 1997) through binding of up to four Gβγ subunits directly to the channel (Whorton and MacKinnon, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Presynaptic opioid receptors inhibit neurotransmitter release through inhibition of VGCCs.
source: In contrast, presynaptic opioid receptors inhibit neurotransmitter release through inhibition of VGCCs (Heinke et al., 2011) or direct inhibition of vesicle release machinery (Blackmer et al., 2001; Gerachshenko et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Presynaptic opioid receptors inhibit neurotransmitter release through direct inhibition of vesicle release machinery.
source: In contrast, presynaptic opioid receptors inhibit neurotransmitter release through inhibition of VGCCs (Heinke et al., 2011) or direct inhibition of vesicle release machinery (Blackmer et al., 2001; Gerachshenko et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: VGCCs can be inhibited by a single Gβγ subunit.
source: Coupling to these presynaptic effectors may be more sensitive since VGCCs can be inhibited by a single Gβγ subunit (Zamponi and Snutch, 1998) and vesicular release is steeply calcium dependent (Katz and Miledi, 1967).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Vesicular release is steeply calcium dependent.
source: Coupling to these presynaptic effectors may be more sensitive since VGCCs can be inhibited by a single Gβγ subunit (Zamponi and Snutch, 1998) and vesicular release is steeply calcium dependent (Katz and Miledi, 1967).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Presynaptic opioid receptor responses have higher sensitivity than postsynaptic responses when directly compared.
source: Consistent with this, presynaptic opioid receptor responses have higher sensitivity than postsynaptic responses when directly compared (Pennock and Hentges, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Postsynaptic receptors desensitize more readily than presynaptic receptors after prolonged exposure to high doses of opioids.
source: Prolonged exposure to high doses of opioids can exacerbate differences in sensitivity since postsynaptic receptors desensitize more readily than presynaptic receptors (Blanchet and Lüscher, 2002; Fyfe et al., 2010; Lowe and Bailey, 2015; Pennock et al., 2012; Rhim et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Postsynaptic opioid receptors on KF neurons are resistant to desensitization.
source: The relative sensitivity of presynaptic and postsynaptic receptors in the pontomedullary circuit identified here will be important to determine, especially since postsynaptic opioid receptors on KF neurons are resistant to desensitization (Levitt and Williams, 2018), suggesting unique receptor regulation in these neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Opioids inhibit an excitatory pontomedullary respiratory circuit by three distinct mechanisms involving presynaptic and postsynaptic opioid receptors in the dorsolateral pons and the ventrolateral medulla.
source: In conclusion, our results show that opioids inhibit an excitatory pontomedullary respiratory circuit by three distinct mechanisms—somatodendritic MORs on dorsolateral pontine and ventrolateral medullary neurons and presynaptic MORs on glutamatergic dorsolateral pontine axon terminals in the ventrolateral medulla—all of which could influence distributed network function and contribute to the profound effects of opioids on breathing.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Vglut2-expressing neurons contain the population of inspiratory rhythm-generating preBötC neurons.
source: We targeted the excitatory vglut2-expressing neurons in the ventrolateral medulla because they contain the populations of inspiratory rhythm-generating preBötC neurons (Wallén-Mackenzie et al., 2006; Gray et al., 2010; Cui et al., 2016) and inspiratory premotor rVRG neurons, and MOR deletion from vglut2 neurons prevents opioid-induced respiratory depression in medullary slices (Sun et al., 2019; Bachmutsky et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: MOR deletion from vglut2 neurons prevents opioid-induced respiratory depression in medullary slices.
source: We targeted the excitatory vglut2-expressing neurons in the ventrolateral medulla because they contain the populations of inspiratory rhythm-generating preBötC neurons (Wallén-Mackenzie et al., 2006; Gray et al., 2010; Cui et al., 2016) and inspiratory premotor rVRG neurons, and MOR deletion from vglut2 neurons prevents opioid-induced respiratory depression in medullary slices (Sun et al., 2019; Bachmutsky et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Genetic deletion or pharmacological blockade of different subsets of pre- and postsynaptic MORs in the dorsolateral pons and preBötC mostly resulted in partial attenuation of opioid-induced respiratory rate suppression.
source: Genetic deletion or pharmacological blockade of different subsets of pre- and postsynaptic MORs in these areas mostly resulted in partial attenuation of opioid-induced respiratory rate suppression, presumably due to redundancy from the subset(s) of MORs in this pontomedullary circuit that were not deleted or blocked.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from prior research findings.

claim: Deletion of MORs from both dorsolateral pons and preBötC did not eliminate morphine-induced respiratory suppression.
source: Furthermore, additional MORs outside of the dorsolateral pontine and preBötC circuit likely contribute to respiratory suppression since deletion of MORs from both dorsolateral pons and preBötC did not eliminate morphine-induced respiratory suppression (Bachmutsky et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The rVRG contains abundant opioid receptors.
source: Often overlooked in the context of opioids, the rVRG contains abundant opioid receptors (Lonergan et al., 2003) and application of an opioid agonist into the rVRG suppresses rate and amplitude of phrenic nerve bursting (Lonergan et al., 2003; Cinelli et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Application of an opioid agonist into the rVRG suppresses rate and amplitude of phrenic nerve bursting.
source: Often overlooked in the context of opioids, the rVRG contains abundant opioid receptors (Lonergan et al., 2003) and application of an opioid agonist into the rVRG suppresses rate and amplitude of phrenic nerve bursting (Lonergan et al., 2003; Cinelli et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Antagonism of opioid receptors in the dorsolateral pons, ventrolateral medulla, and caudal medullary raphe was able to eliminate remifentanil-induced respiratory depression.
source: Another potential contributor to OIRD are the caudal medullary raphe nuclei since antagonism of opioid receptors in the dorsolateral pons, ventrolateral medulla, and caudal medullary raphe was able to eliminate remifentanil-induced respiratory depression (Palkovic et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.
